technique: sound — the consonants and vowels doing quiet work, worth saying aloud
lesson:
Today we work on one thing: sound. Sound means the actual noise the letters make when you say the words out loud, the consonants and the vowels.

This poem repeats consonant sounds close together. Say "catching on the fence wire" and you hear the hard "c" and "ch" and the short "e" packed tight. Say "slow, reluctant, catching" and the "l" sounds slide. Say "the kind that doesn't ask" and the "k" and "d" sounds knock against each other.

Here is why it works on a listener, said plainly. Hard sounds like "k" and "d" make you stop your mouth and start again, so the line feels like work. Soft sounds like "l" let the line move without stopping. Your mouth copies the poem's meaning while you read.

Try this: read your draft out loud and mark every word that makes your mouth stop short.

The second time through, listen for the hard "k" sound in "cold," "kettle," and "So — up!"

Here is the poem.
poem:
The fog comes off the low field like it's being peeled,
slow, reluctant, catching on the fence wire
and letting go, and the wind that follows after
has a working sound to it, the kind that doesn't ask—
it just leans on the maples till they give
their last red handful to the ground. You've learned
the look of things half-settled, a door propped open
you'll get to closing, a word you're owed and waiting on,
the way a gray sky can't decide if it will rain
or only think about it all the morning long.
No matter. There's wood to split and a cold stove
and a list that won't read itself in the dark.

The kettle's cold and the quiet's yours alone for a while yet—

So — up!
